title: The small friar (1542–1591)
hook: barely five feet tall; Teresa joked he was half a friar

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's nine lines: breviary. Your line was god alone is enough. Where did you put your card? Today, a new part of the path, and the friend Teresa loved and teased. Day two hundred fifty-four.

Teresa of Ávila has spent years founding reformed convents of Carmelite nuns. Now she wants to do the same for the men, and start a house of friars living the old, strict, prayerful way. She has found exactly two volunteers. One is an older priest, a solid, respectable man. The other is a young priest in his twenties, thin, quiet, and very short. She's delighted with both. And, the story goes, she joked that she now had a friar and a half to begin with. Today's word is the half.
screen: `TERESA WANTS FRIARS TOO.` → `TWO VOLUNTEERS.` → `A FRIAR AND A HALF.`

segments.voice: The half was John of the Cross. For the next eighteen days, this part of our path follows him. First, the size. Accounts put him at a little under five feet tall. Small, thin, often ill. He'd go on to write poems and books on prayer that are still read. But on the day Teresa met him, what people saw first was how little he was. Second, the joke. Teresa teased the people she loved. The friar-and-a-half line is affectionate, not cruel. She also nicknamed him her little Seneca, after the Roman philosopher, a fond joke about how serious and wise he was. Third, what she really thought. In a letter, Teresa wrote that though he was small, she understood him to be great in the eyes of God. It's an old pattern in the Bible. When the prophet Samuel goes looking for Israel's next king, he's impressed by the eldest brother's looks and height. And God tells him not to look at height or appearance, because people look at the outside and God looks at the heart. The king turns out to be the youngest son, out in the field with the sheep. Fourth, what comes. This small man would be kidnapped by his own order, locked in a closet-sized cell, escape through a window, and write a poem about a dark night that people still read. He was named a saint and a Doctor of the Church. And it all began with a joke about his height.
screen: `JUST UNDER FIVE FEET TALL.` · `A FRIAR AND A HALF.` · `GREAT IN THE EYES OF GOD.` · `A SAINT, A POET, A TEACHER.` · then, large: `GOD LOOKS AT THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice greatness in someone small. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone easy to overlook. A quiet coworker, a child, an old neighbor, the person who cleans your building. Picture their face. What do they carry that nobody sees? What do they do well? If you pray, you can hold them before God for a moment. If you don't, just let yourself see them the way someone who loves them would. The bell holds the time.
Little Seneca. Teresa's fond nickname for John of the Cross, a small, serious friar she also called great in the eyes of God. Today's word.
Your line: half a friar. Today, say one true, specific word of praise to someone people usually overlook. Day two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint John of the Cross on his feast day, December 14; Carmelite friars and nuns especially read his poems and books, and many Catholics know him through his teaching on the dark night.

what it means: a small, sickly young priest whom Teresa teased, trusted and saw as great in God's eyes.

notes: 'A friar and a half' (fraile y medio) is a traditional anecdote about Teresa's first two friars, Antonio de Heredia and John; confirm source and whether it is in her writings or early biographies. Presented as 'the story goes'.
'Senequita' (little Seneca) nickname: in a letter of Teresa (c. 1568); confirm.
Teresa's remark that though he is small he is great in the eyes of God: letter to Francisco de Salcedo, September 1568; paraphrased. Confirm.
Height: commonly given as about 4'11" (under five feet); stated as 'accounts put him'.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'Spain, 1568' from the hook (Teresa met John in 1567, the year day 256 uses, and the friar-and-a-half remark is usually placed then); cut the superlatives 'one of the greatest poets in the Spanish language', 'closest partner' and 'read in every language', and the 'retold for four hundred years' claim; fixed the Samuel story (the text has Samuel impressed by the eldest, Eliab, not by 'tall, handsome brothers'); replaced the superlative myth item with a Samuel item; replaced the trapdoor dates (canonized 1726, Doctor 1926, not in the cited texts) with the Senequita detail. Keeper: confirm whether 'fraile y medio' is in Foundations ch. 3 itself; if so the script can say Teresa wrote it.
